```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(forcats)
library(rsample)
library(nnet)

survey <- read.csv("data/sleep_survey.csv") |>
  mutate(early_class = if_else(has_early_class == "Yes", 1, 0))

rmse <- function(actual, predicted) sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))

# Same split as the "Prepare and split" slide, so later slides run on their own
model_data <- survey |>
  select(avg_grade, early_class, program, study_hours_week,
         sleep_hours, stress_level, work_hours_week) |>
  drop_na()

set.seed(100)
data_split <- initial_split(model_data, prop = 0.80)
train <- training(data_split)
test  <- testing(data_split)
```

## Today's Participation Credit

1. Sit with your project group.
2. Choose **one numeric** and **one categorical** response from your data.
3. For each response, compare a **baseline** with at least **two models**.
4. Ask an AI to do the same analysis, then compare it with yours.
5. Knit into a *pdf* and submit to Gradescope (make sure that everyone's name is in the submission).


## Choosing your two responses {.smaller}

| | Part A | Part B |
|---|---|---|
| **Response** | Numeric | Categorical |
| **Model** | `lm()` | `glm()` (2 categories) or `multinom()` (3 or more) |
| **Baseline** | Training average | Most common training category |
| **Score** | RMSE (smaller is better) | Accuracy (bigger is better) |

::: {.callout-note title="Write one sentence for each"}
"We want to predict ___ for a new ___ because ___."
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="No categorical column?"}
Make one, such as high / low from a numeric column. Then do **not** use that numeric column as a predictor.
:::


## Choosing your predictors {.smaller}

You may use **as many explanatory variables as you like**, but:

- No ID numbers or names
- Nothing that gives away the answer
- Nothing you would not know at the time of prediction (this includes your other response)
- Avoid predictors that carry almost the same information (multicollinearity)
- Be able to give a short reason for your choices

::: {.callout-important title="More is not always better"}
A model with many predictors can fit the training data closely and still do worse on new data (**overfitting**).
:::


# The toolbox

## How the toolbox works

::: {.callout-note title="These use the sleep survey, not your data"}
Click **Run Code**, then change the predictors and see what happens.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Your job"}
Replace the data and column names with your own.
:::


## Prepare and split {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note title="`select()`, `drop_na()`, `initial_split()`"}
Keep the columns you need, drop incomplete rows, then split **once**. All models use the same split.
:::

```{webr}
model_data <- survey |>
  select(avg_grade, early_class, program, study_hours_week,
         sleep_hours, stress_level, work_hours_week) |>
  drop_na()

set.seed(100)
data_split <- initial_split(model_data, prop = 0.80)
train <- training(data_split)
test  <- testing(data_split)

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```


## Part A: the baseline

::: {.callout-note title="`rmse()`"}
The typical size of an error, in the same units as the response. The baseline guesses the training average for everyone.
:::

```{webr}
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))

baseline <- mean(train$avg_grade)

rmse(train$avg_grade, baseline)    # training score
rmse(test$avg_grade, baseline)     # test score
```


## Part A: two linear models {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note title="`lm()` and `predict()`"}
Fit on the **training** set only. Then score on both sets.
:::

```{webr}
fit1 <- lm(avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program, data = train)
fit2 <- lm(avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program + sleep_hours +
             stress_level + work_hours_week, data = train)

rmse(train$avg_grade, predict(fit1, train))
rmse(test$avg_grade,  predict(fit1, test))

rmse(train$avg_grade, predict(fit2, train))
rmse(test$avg_grade,  predict(fit2, test))

coef(fit1)    # pick one slope and explain it in words
```


## Part B: the baseline

::: {.callout-note title="Always guess the most common category"}
Find it using the **training** set, then check how often that guess is right.
:::

```{webr}
train |> count(early_class)

most_common <- names(which.max(table(train$early_class)))
most_common

mean(train$early_class == most_common)    # training accuracy
mean(test$early_class == most_common)     # test accuracy
```


## Part B: two categories {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note title="`glm(..., family = binomial)`"}
Logistic regression. The response must be **0 or 1**. Predict 1 when the probability is above 0.5.
:::

```{webr}
logit_fit <- glm(early_class ~ sleep_hours + stress_level,
                 data = train, family = binomial)

prob_train <- predict(logit_fit, train, type = "response")
prob_test  <- predict(logit_fit, test,  type = "response")

pred_train <- if_else(prob_train > 0.5, 1, 0)
pred_test  <- if_else(prob_test > 0.5, 1, 0)

mean(pred_train == train$early_class)    # training accuracy
mean(pred_test == test$early_class)      # test accuracy

table(actual = test$early_class, predicted = pred_test)
```

- Text such as "Yes" / "No"? Convert it **before** splitting: `if_else(x == "Yes", 1, 0)`


## Part B: three or more categories {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note title="`multinom()` from the `nnet` package"}
`predict()` gives the predicted category directly. No cutoff needed.
:::

```{webr}
multi_fit <- multinom(program ~ avg_grade + study_hours_week,
                      data = train, trace = FALSE)

mean(predict(multi_fit, train) == train$program)    # training accuracy
mean(predict(multi_fit, test) == test$program)      # test accuracy

table(actual = test$program, predicted = predict(multi_fit, test))

# The baseline for this response
top_program <- names(which.max(table(train$program)))
mean(test$program == top_program)
```


## Common problems {.smaller}

| What you see | What to try |
|---|---|
| `could not find function "initial_split"` | `library(rsample)` |
| `object not found` | Check the spelling, and that you kept the column in `select()` |
| `y values must be 0 <= y <= 1` | Convert your response to 0 / 1 |
| `factor ... has new levels` | Combine rare categories **before** splitting, e.g. `fct_lump_min(x, min = 10)` |
| Very few rows left | `drop_na()` is using a column with many missing values. Do you need it? |

# Part C: You vs. AI

## Lock in your work first

::: {.callout-important title="Before opening any AI"}
Your predictors, tables and chosen models from Parts A and B must be written down. **Do not change them afterwards.**
:::

- Use any AI chatbot (e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot). One per group is enough.
- Share **column names, types and a short description** only. Do **not** upload your data or any personal information.
- If you cannot or prefer not to use AI, ask me for a sample AI response to critique.


## The prompt

Copy this, fill in the blanks, and paste it into the AI:

::: {.callout-note title="Starter prompt" icon="false"}
I have a dataset about ___. The columns are ___ (with types). In R, predict ___ (numeric) and ___ (categorical). Use `initial_split()` with an 80/20 split and `set.seed(100)`. Compare your models with a baseline, report training and test scores, and explain your choices.
:::

- You may ask follow-up questions. Keep a copy of what you typed.


## Do not take its word for it

1. **Run the AI's code** in your Rmd. Report the scores that *R* gives you.
2. Did it use the same rows, seed and split as you? If not, can you compare the scores fairly?
3. Look for anything questionable:
    - an ID column or a give-away predictor
    - judging a model on training data only
    - claims that one variable *causes* another
    - methods or functions you do not understand


## Your comparison {.smaller}

| | Ours | AI's |
|---|---|---|
| Predictors (Part A) | | |
| Predictors (Part B) | | |
| Test RMSE | | |
| Test accuracy | | |

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer these"}
1. **One thing the AI did better** than you
2. **One thing the AI did worse** than you
3. **One thing you would change** in your own analysis, or why you would not
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Show your evidence"}
Point to a specific line of code, number or sentence. "The AI was more detailed" is not enough.

You are marked on your comparison, **not** on whether you beat the AI.
:::
